types.name: Force on a current-carrying conductor
types.method: The force on a wire at right angles to a magnetic field is magnetic flux density multiplied by current multiplied by the length of wire in the field. B is in tesla, I in amps and l in metres, so change cm to m (divide by 100) first. The equation is on the equation sheet; to find B, I or l, divide F by the other two.
commonErrors: Leaving the length in cm, so the force is 100 times too big
Mixing up B (flux density, in T) and F (force, in N)
Forgetting that the force is zero if the wire runs along the field rather than across it

worked.question: A straight wire 0.5 m long carries a current of 3 A at right angles to a magnetic field of flux density 0.4 T. Calculate the force on the wire.
steps: Known: B = 0.4 T, I = 3 A, l = 0.5 m. Unknown: F.

practice.question: In a lab experiment a wire 0.4 m long rests on a top-pan balance between the poles of a magnet. The flux density is 0.1 T and the wire carries 2.5 A at right angles to the field. Calculate the force on the wire.
practice.hint: Use F = B × I × l with the values as given.
walkthrough: B = 0.1 T, I = 2.5 A, l = 0.4 m, find F.

practice.question: The coil of a loudspeaker has 1.2 m of wire in a radial magnetic field of flux density 0.5 T. The current in the coil is 0.3 A. Calculate the force on the coil.
practice.hint: Force equals flux density multiplied by current multiplied by length.
walkthrough: B = 0.5 T, I = 0.3 A, l = 1.2 m, find F.

practice.question: A wire 0.2 m long in the gap of an electromagnet carries a current of 1.5 A and experiences a force of 0.06 N. Calculate the magnetic flux density in the gap.
practice.hint: Rearrange F = B × I × l to B = F / (I × l).
walkthrough: F = B × I × l → B = F / (I × l)

practice.question: One side of the coil in a toy car motor is 8 cm long and carries a current of 5 A in a field of flux density 0.15 T. Calculate the force on that side of the coil.
practice.hint: Change 8 cm to metres before using F = B × I × l.
walkthrough: B = 0.15 T, I = 5 A, l = 8 cm = 0.08 m, find F.

practice.question: A 30 cm length of wire in a crane motor sits in a field of flux density 0.2 T. The force on the wire is 0.12 N. Calculate the current in the wire.
practice.hint: Convert 30 cm to metres, then rearrange to I = F / (B × l).
walkthrough: F = B × I × l → I = F / (B × l)

practice.question: A 0.5 m length of wire on a model train has a resistance of 2 Ω and is connected across a 6 V supply. The wire is at right angles to a field of flux density 0.1 T. Calculate the force on the wire.
practice.hint: Find the current first with I = V / R, then use F = B × I × l.
walkthrough: V = 6 V, R = 2 Ω, B = 0.1 T, l = 0.5 m, find F.
First the current: I = V / R = 6 / 2 = 3 A

types.name: Transformer turns ratio
types.method: The ratio of the p.d.s across the two coils equals the ratio of the numbers of turns. Write the equation as a pair of fractions, put in the three values you know, and solve for the fourth: V_s = V_p × N_s / N_p, N_s = N_p × V_s / V_p, and so on. A step-up transformer has more turns on the secondary and a larger output p.d.; a step-down transformer has fewer.
commonErrors: Putting primary on top of one fraction and secondary on top of the other
Expecting a step-down transformer to give a bigger p.d. out
Mixing kV and V in the same fraction

worked.question: A mains adapter contains a transformer with 2300 turns on the primary coil and 120 turns on the secondary coil. The primary is connected to the 230 V mains. Calculate the output potential difference.
steps: Known: V_p = 230 V, N_p = 2300, N_s = 120. Unknown: V_s.
V_p / V_s = N_p / N_s → V_s = V_p × N_s / N_p

practice.question: A lab transformer has 100 turns on the primary coil and 500 turns on the secondary coil. The input is 12 V a.c. Calculate the output potential difference.
practice.hint: V_s = V_p × N_s / N_p; more secondary turns means a bigger output.
walkthrough: V_p = 12 V, N_p = 100, N_s = 500, find V_s.

practice.question: The transformer in a phone charger has 1150 turns on the primary and 25 turns on the secondary. It is plugged into the 230 V mains. Calculate the output potential difference.
practice.hint: Use V_s = V_p × N_s / N_p.

practice.question: A doorbell transformer steps the 230 V mains down to 8 V. The primary coil has 920 turns. Calculate the number of turns on the secondary coil.
practice.hint: Rearrange the turns ratio to N_s = N_p × V_s / V_p.
walkthrough: V_p = 230 V, V_s = 8 V, N_p = 920, find N_s.
V_p / V_s = N_p / N_s → N_s = N_p × V_s / V_p

practice.question: A laptop charger steps the 230 V mains down to 20 V. The secondary coil has 40 turns. Calculate the number of turns on the primary coil.
practice.hint: Rearrange the turns ratio to N_p = N_s × V_p / V_s.
walkthrough: V_p = 230 V, V_s = 20 V, N_s = 40, find N_p.
V_p / V_s = N_p / N_s → N_p = N_s × V_p / V_s

practice.question: A step-up transformer at a power station raises the p.d. from 25 kV to 400 kV. Its primary coil has 1500 turns. Calculate the number of turns on the secondary coil.
practice.hint: Both p.d.s are in kV so the ratio works as it stands; use N_s = N_p × V_s / V_p.
walkthrough: V_p = 25 kV, V_s = 400 kV, N_p = 1500, find N_s.

practice.question: The transformer in a model railway controller has 2000 turns in total. 1600 of them are on the primary coil, which is connected to the 230 V mains. Calculate the output potential difference.
practice.hint: Find the number of secondary turns first, then use V_s = V_p × N_s / N_p.
walkthrough: V_p = 230 V, N_p = 1600, total turns 2000, find V_s.

types.name: Transformer power
types.method: For a transformer that is 100% efficient the power into the primary equals the power out of the secondary, so V_p × I_p = V_s × I_s. Put in the three values you know and divide to find the fourth. If a p.d. is missing, find it from the turns ratio first. Stepping the p.d. up steps the current down by the same factor.
commonErrors: Expecting the current to go up when the p.d. goes up
Forgetting to change mA to A before multiplying
Using the turns ratio with currents as if currents were p.d.s

worked.question: A transformer connected to the 230 V mains takes a primary current of 0.5 A. The output p.d. is 23 V. Assuming the transformer is 100% efficient, calculate the current in the secondary coil.
steps: Known: V_p = 230 V, I_p = 0.5 A, V_s = 23 V. Unknown: I_s.
V_p × I_p = V_s × I_s → I_s = V_p × I_p / V_s

practice.question: A lab step-up transformer has an input of 12 V at 2 A and an output p.d. of 48 V. Assuming it is 100% efficient, calculate the output current.
practice.hint: Power in equals power out: I_s = V_p × I_p / V_s.
walkthrough: V_p = 12 V, I_p = 2 A, V_s = 48 V, find I_s.

practice.question: A games console adapter is connected to the 230 V mains and supplies 11.5 V at 6 A. Assuming the transformer inside is 100% efficient, calculate the current drawn from the mains.
practice.hint: Rearrange V_p × I_p = V_s × I_s to I_p = V_s × I_s / V_p.
walkthrough: V_p = 230 V, V_s = 11.5 V, I_s = 6 A, find I_p.

practice.question: A phone charger takes a current of 20 mA from the 230 V mains and supplies the phone at 5 V. Assuming the transformer is 100% efficient, calculate the current supplied to the phone. Give your answer in amps.
practice.hint: Change 20 mA to amps first, then use I_s = V_p × I_p / V_s.
walkthrough: V_p = 230 V, I_p = 20 mA = 0.02 A, V_s = 5 V, find I_s.

practice.question: A transformer for a set of halogen lights takes 0.2 A from the 230 V mains and supplies the lamps with a current of 4 A. Assuming it is 100% efficient, calculate the p.d. across the lamps.
practice.hint: Rearrange V_p × I_p = V_s × I_s to V_s = V_p × I_p / I_s.
walkthrough: V_p = 230 V, I_p = 0.2 A, I_s = 4 A, find V_s.

practice.question: A garden-lighting transformer has 1000 turns on the primary and 50 turns on the secondary. It is connected to the 230 V mains and the lights draw 2 A from the secondary. Assuming the transformer is 100% efficient, calculate the current in the primary coil.
practice.hint: Find the secondary p.d. from the turns ratio first, then use I_p = V_s × I_s / V_p.
walkthrough: V_p = 230 V, N_p = 1000, N_s = 50, I_s = 2 A, find I_p.
First the output p.d.: V_s = V_p × N_s / N_p = 230 × 50 / 1000 = 11.5 V

practice.question: A lab step-up transformer with 60 turns on the primary and 1200 turns on the secondary is connected to a 12 V a.c. supply. The primary current is 5 A. Assuming the transformer is 100% efficient, calculate the current in the secondary coil.
practice.hint: Use the turns ratio to find V_s, then I_s = V_p × I_p / V_s.
walkthrough: V_p = 12 V, N_p = 60, N_s = 1200, I_p = 5 A, find I_s.
First the output p.d.: V_s = V_p × N_s / N_p = 12 × 1200 / 60 = 240 V

types.name: Power loss in transmission cables
types.method: The power wasted as heat in a cable is current squared multiplied by the resistance of the cable. If the question gives the power being transmitted and the transmission p.d., find the current first from I = P / V, then square it and multiply by the cable resistance. Stepping the p.d. up by a factor cuts the current by the same factor and the loss by that factor squared.
commonErrors: Using the transmission p.d. in P = I × V to find the loss instead of the cable's resistance
Leaving the transmitted power in kW when finding the current

worked.question: A transmission cable has a total resistance of 5 Ω and carries a current of 20 A. Calculate the power wasted as heat in the cable.
steps: Known: I = 20 A, R = 5 Ω. Unknown: P lost.

practice.question: An overhead line supplying a farm has a resistance of 0.5 Ω and carries a current of 40 A. Calculate the power lost in the line.
practice.hint: Use P = I² × R; square the current first.
walkthrough: I = 40 A, R = 0.5 Ω, find P lost.

practice.question: A section of power line has a resistance of 10 Ω. It carries a current of 50 A. Calculate the power wasted in this section.
practice.hint: Power lost equals current squared multiplied by resistance.
walkthrough: I = 50 A, R = 10 Ω, find P lost.

practice.question: The cable from a wind turbine has a resistance of 2 Ω and wastes 1800 W as heat. Calculate the current in the cable.
practice.hint: Rearrange P = I² × R to I² = P / R, then take the square root.
walkthrough: P = 1800 W, R = 2 Ω, find I.

practice.question: A power line has a resistance of 0.05 Ω for every kilometre of its length. The line is 20 km long and carries a current of 60 A. Calculate the power lost in the line.
practice.hint: Find the total resistance of the 20 km first, then use P = I² × R.
walkthrough: Resistance per km = 0.05 Ω, length 20 km, I = 60 A, find P lost.

practice.question: A small hydroelectric generator transmits 100 kW of power at 2000 V through cables of total resistance 4 Ω. Calculate the power lost in the cables. Give your answer in kW.
practice.hint: Find the current first with I = P / V (power in watts), then use P = I² × R and change to kW.
walkthrough: P transmitted = 100 kW = 100 000 W, V = 2000 V, R = 4 Ω, find P lost.
First the current: I = P / V = 100 000 / 2000 = 50 A

practice.question: A factory is supplied with 60 kW of power through cables of total resistance 0.4 Ω. At 400 V the power lost in the cables is 9000 W. A transformer is fitted so the same 60 kW is transmitted at 4000 V instead. Calculate the power lost in the cables now.
practice.hint: Find the new, smaller current from I = P / V at 4000 V, then use P = I² × R.
walkthrough: P transmitted = 60 kW = 60 000 W, new V = 4000 V, R = 0.4 Ω, find the new P lost.
New current: I = P / V = 60 000 / 4000 = 15 A
P lost = 90 W (down from 9000 W: ten times the p.d., one hundredth of the loss)
